chunks: What al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from a group who heard him saying.

Indeed, smiling during salat (prayer) does not invalidate the salat (prayer), nor does it invalidate the wudu (ablution). Rather, it is only laughter containing loud guffawing that cuts off the salat (prayer).

His statement, peace be upon him (AS), 'Rather, it is only laughter containing loud guffawing that cuts off,' refers back to the salat (prayer) and not to the wudu (ablution). Do you not see that he said, 'laughter containing loud guffawing cuts off,' and 'cutting off' is only said regarding salat (prayer), because it is not customary for one to say, 'the wudu (ablution) was cut off'; rather, it is said, 'the salat (prayer) was cut off.'
And it is possible that the two reports were issued in the context of taqiyyah, because they accord with the doctrines of some of the ʿāmmah.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation or precautionary conformity in a sensitive context
key_terms.الضَّحِكُ: laughter as distinct from mere smiling
key_terms.الْعَامَّةِ: the general Sunni majority, in contrast to Shia usage
key_terms.الْقَطْعُ: invalidation or interruption, here of salat (prayer)

ai.seo_question: Does smiling or laughing during salat (prayer) invalidate the salat (prayer) or wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling of smiling and laughing during salat (prayer), stating that smiling does not invalidate either salat (prayer) or wudu (ablution), while loud laughter invalidates the salat (prayer). The accompanying explanation clarifies that the expression 'cuts off' applies to salat (prayer), not wudu (ablution), and also notes the possibility of taqiyyah in the wording of the reports.
